title: Where is thy sting (1 Corinthians 15:51–57)
hook: O death, where is thy victory

segments.voice: Yesterday, enigma: seeing now in a dark manner, and the hope of seeing face to face. Your line was then, face to face.

Some people in Corinth had decided the dead don't rise. Souls might go on, they thought, but bodies? Bodies rot. Paul answers them in chapter fifteen, and it's an argument most of the way through: he reasons, lists the people who saw the risen Christ, talks about seeds and harvest. Then, near the end, the argument turns into something more like a song. He starts taunting death itself, as if it were a bully that's finally been beaten.
screen: `SOME SAY THE DEAD DON'T RISE.` → `PAUL ANSWERS IN CHAPTER FIFTEEN.` → `AN ARGUMENT TURNS INTO A SONG.`

segments.voice: He begins with a secret: "Behold, I tell you a mystery." Then the Douay-Rheims, following the Latin Vulgate, reads: "We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed." Bibles translated from the Greek put it the other way round: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed. The copies of the letter differ here, and translators follow the text they have. Either way, Paul's point stands: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible. Then he borrows from the prophet Hosea and makes it a dare: "O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?" The Greek for sting is kentron: the stinger of a bee or a scorpion, and also the goad a farmer used to drive an ox. Paul names the stinger: the sting of death is sin. Preachers sometimes add a picture: a bee that stings once leaves its stinger behind. In that picture, death stung Christ, and lost its sting. And Paul doesn't end with a final argument. He ends with thanks: "But thanks be to God, who hath given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Catholics hear this chapter at funerals and confess it every Sunday in the Creed: I look forward to the resurrection of the dead. The Church never pretends death doesn't hurt. A few verses earlier, Paul himself calls death an enemy, the last one to be destroyed. An enemy, but a beaten one.
screen: `A MYSTERY: WE SHALL BE CHANGED.` · `TWO READINGS OF ONE VERSE.` · `KENTRON: THE STINGER, THE GOAD.` · `THANKS BE TO GOD: THE VICTORY.` · then, large: `O DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?`

segments.voice: Hold in mind someone who is dying, or very old, or very sick, someone you know or have only heard about; if that's too close today, think of everyone in the world who will die tonight, and picture them with care. If you pray, use your own words, or the Hail Mary, which asks Mary to pray for us now and at the hour of our death. If you don't, wish them peace.
Kentron. The Greek word for a stinger or an ox-goad: Paul's taunt at death, whose sting, sin, Christ has drawn. Today's word.
Your line: death, where is thy sting. Paul ends with thanks. Day five hundred seventy-six, done.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dying, and the Church offers the anointing of the sick and Viaticum, a last Communion; 1 Corinthians 15 is among the readings for a Catholic funeral.

trapdoor: what you thought: a brave saying for funerals.
what it means: Paul taunts death because Christ is risen, and the dead will rise changed.
what a scholar hears: kentron, the goad and the stinger; Hosea 13:14 reworked; and a famous variant reading in 15:51 between Greek and Latin copies.

chat.says: Do Catholics really believe our bodies will rise again someday?
options: Yes: Paul says the dead will rise incorruptible; the Creed says it too.
No, only the soul lives on; the body is left behind for good.
Only the saints' bodies rise; everyone else goes on as a soul.
chat.meaning: Paul answers Corinth: the dead will rise incorruptible. Catholics confess the resurrection of the dead in the Creed every Sunday.

kentron.meaning: Greek: a sting, or a farmer's ox-goad

notes: 1 Corinthians 15 (58 verses) as the letter's longest chapter. Confirm.
Variant at 15:51: the Vulgate reading ('omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur') vs. the majority Greek reading. Stated neutrally; confirm the Douay-Rheims wording.
The bee-stinger image is described as a preachers' illustration, not as the meaning of the text.
Creed wording 'I look forward to the resurrection of the dead' is the current English Missal; paraphrased, not cited as a quotation. Confirm.
Practice is about someone near death; gentle alternative offered for listeners in fresh grief.
